speaker_instructions.Narrator: Warm, intimate, grounded storytelling. Follow Roger’s emotions without preaching. Allow recognition, shame, relief, and gratitude to register through natural variation and unhurried pauses.
speaker_instructions.Roger: A humble, courageous protagonist. Warm, human, expressive conversation with varied pitch and rhythm. Let vulnerability, curiosity, joy, and growing conviction emerge as appropriate to the line. Never a booming announcer or a monotone. In prayers, speak to God personally. Remembrance is woven into ordinary life, not delivered as a sermon. Let fear and trust coexist.
speaker_instructions.Mother: A mature older mother speaking to her adult son. Warm, gently weathered, affectionate, practical and reassuring. Understated, not theatrical.
speaker_instructions.Rita: Gentle and sincere, with quiet conviction and self-respect. Natural, warm conversation.
speaker_instructions.Tim: An ordinary working man. Friendly and direct, with natural warmth. Let frustration or relief follow the meaning of the line.
speaker_instructions.Rick: A successful middle-aged man, kindly and confident. Speak to the craftsman with respect and natural curiosity.
speaker_instructions.Katie: An assured adult woman, elegant, friendly and candid. Natural conversation, never an advertisement.
speaker_instructions.Katie’s father: An experienced older businessman giving patient, practical advice. Conversational, not an announcer.
speaker_instructions.Factory manager: A gruff factory manager, skeptical and dismissive but believable. No shouting or exaggerated villain voice.
speaker_instructions.Coworker: A skeptical coworker teasing another man with dry disbelief. Natural, not cartoonish.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: The first man laughed before Roger had finished speaking.

turns.speaker: Coworker
turns.text: You’re going to make shoes for private customers?

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Roger stood beside his workbench, a length of waxed thread caught around his finger. Around him, the factory carried on: belts turning, needles striking leather, soles dropping into wooden bins.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I want to try,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
he said.

Someone at the next bench grinned.

turns.speaker: Coworker
turns.text: Listen to him. He’ll have his name above a shop by Christmas.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger tried to smile with them.

His manager did not smile.

turns.speaker: Factory manager
turns.text: And who feeds your mother while you’re trying?

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
That quietened the room.

The manager glanced toward the door, where men gathered every morning hoping someone would miss a shift.

turns.speaker: Factory manager
turns.text: You have work here, Roger. Don’t throw away what you have for something you’ve imagined.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Roger looked down at his hands. A fine white scar crossed one knuckle. Dark wax had settled into the creases of his fingers.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I understand,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
he said.

He returned to his stitching.

For the rest of the afternoon, whenever laughter rose above the machines, he wondered whether it was about him.

He kept his head bent so that nobody would see his face. Anger came first, then shame at how badly he wanted their approval.

Beneath the noise of the machines, he turned inward.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: God, You know how small I feel. Please don’t let their words become the limits I place on You.
turns.instruction: A personal prayer addressed to God. Speak as a real man in this moment, with vulnerability, longing, gratitude or growing trust as the words imply. Expressive and understated, never preaching. No whispering.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: He pulled the next stitch through. His hands were still unsteady. He asked for help again.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
At home, his mother divided a pot of stew among four bowls.

His youngest brother had torn the sole of his school shoe. His sister needed money for an examination fee. A notice from the landlord lay beneath the salt jar, folded so that only the amount due was visible.

Roger put his wages on the table.

His mother counted them once, then began making small piles.

He watched her move a coin from one pile to another.

He wanted to take her hands in his and tell her she would never have to do this again. But he could not even promise next month’s rent.

His throat tightened. He went outside before she could ask why.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: God, I don’t know how to give them the life I want for them. I have so little. I know so little.
turns.instruction: A personal prayer addressed to God. Speak as a real man in this moment, with vulnerability, longing, gratitude or growing trust as the words imply. Expressive and understated, never preaching. No whispering.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
For a while, that was all he could say.

Then he remembered whom he was asking. The little he held in his hands was not the measure of what God could give. God’s knowledge did not end where his knowledge ended. God’s generosity was not exhausted because Roger could not yet see an opening.

He stayed there until he could breathe more easily. The rent was still due. But he no longer felt that he had to face it entirely alone.

For years, he had called this his fate.

There was dignity in work. His mother had taught him that. He did not resent the stitching, or the men beside him, or the honest tiredness in his shoulders at the end of a day.

But somewhere along the way, he had begun to believe that accepting his circumstances was the same thing as accepting God’s will.

He prayed for enough work.

He prayed not to fall ill.

He rarely prayed for anything larger.

He had begun to bring the same small picture of the world into every prayer: so much money, so many jobs, a few fortunate people, and everyone else waiting for what remained.

Yet he believed the One he prayed to was infinite.

The contradiction unsettled him. He could see the end of his wages. He could not see the end of God’s abundance. Why had he been treating them as though they were the same thing?

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Help me stop mistaking the edge of what I can see for the edge of what You can make possible.
turns.instruction: A personal prayer addressed to God. Speak as a real man in this moment, with vulnerability, longing, gratitude or growing trust as the words imply. Expressive and understated, never preaching. No whispering.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: A week earlier, outside the factory, he had watched a well-dressed man remove an expensive shoe and rub his heel. The man had complained bitterly to his companion.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Third pair this month. Every shop promises they’ll soften.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger had noticed the stiff edge at the back of the shoe. He had known two ways he might alter it.

He had said nothing.

That silence troubled him more than the manager’s laughter.

Someone had needed something he might have been able to give, and he had stood there waiting to become the sort of man who was allowed to offer it.

That evening, after his siblings had gone to bed, his mother found him repairing the school shoe.

turns.speaker: Mother
turns.text: What happened?

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He told her.

She listened without interrupting.

Then she asked,

turns.speaker: Mother
turns.text: Can you begin without leaving us hungry?

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger looked up.

It was such a different question from whether he would succeed.

Over the following weeks, he put aside a little money, bought discarded leather with permission, and repaired shoes after supper. He kept taking factory shifts. On evenings and the occasional day he could spare, he went out to speak to people.

Before the first outing, he sat on the edge of his bed with his coat already on.

His heart was beating as though something dangerous waited outside.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: God,
turns.instruction: A sincere private prayer. Let the specific meaning guide the emotion: fear, longing, gratitude or trust. Clearly voiced, not whispered or sermon-like.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: he whispered,

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: help me see where I can be useful. And help me speak when I see it.
turns.instruction: A sincere private prayer. Let the specific meaning guide the emotion: fear, longing, gratitude or trust. Clearly voiced, not whispered or sermon-like.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Then he stood up.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He began badly.

He spoke too quickly. He explained things people had not asked about. When someone said they were busy, he apologized so many times that they became impatient.

A shopkeeper asked where his business was.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I work from home.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
The man’s expression changed.

A hotel clerk looked at Roger’s worn shoes and said their guests already had suppliers.

One woman listened politely, then asked whether he could mend her gardener’s boots.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Yes,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger said.

He took the boots.

By the end of the first month, he had learned something unexpected.

Being dismissed was unpleasant. It was not unbearable.

After one rejection, he stopped around the corner and pressed his palms together to keep them from trembling.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Stay with me in this, God. Help me meet the next person without carrying my hurt into their doorway.
turns.instruction: A personal prayer addressed to God. Speak as a real man in this moment, with vulnerability, longing, gratitude or growing trust as the words imply. Expressive and understated, never preaching. No whispering.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
On another day, someone offered him a chair and a few minutes. He silently gave thanks before sitting down. Nothing had been sold. Still, there was something here to receive: time, attention, a person willing to speak to him.

He could be embarrassed at eleven in the morning and still eat lunch at noon. He could hear no, walk to the next street, and discover that the world had not ended.

Gradually, he stopped beginning with what he wanted to sell.

He began asking questions.

Which shoes did people wear longest? What wore out first? When did their feet begin to hurt? Which pair did they keep buying, and what did they wish someone would change?

Some people hurried away.

Others had been waiting years for someone to ask.

Walking home, Roger began to notice how much he had passed without seeing: a broken fastening someone had learned to tolerate, a shopkeeper who knew a supplier, a craftsman willing to explain a mistake.

God’s abundance was becoming less abstract to him. There was knowledge he had not learned, help he had not asked for, usefulness he had not discovered. He had been living among possibilities while telling himself there were none.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Thank You for helping me notice.
turns.instruction: A personal prayer addressed to God. Speak as a real man in this moment, with vulnerability, longing, gratitude or growing trust as the words imply. Expressive and understated, never preaching. No whispering.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Tim was leaning against a car outside a café when Roger met him.

One shoe was off. His socked foot rested on the curb.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Long day?

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Roger asked.

turns.speaker: Tim
turns.text: Long enough.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Tim was a chauffeur. Most days he drove across the city, waited, drove again, then stood beside the car while other people finished their evenings.

turns.speaker: Tim
turns.text: My left foot’s fine,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: he said.

turns.speaker: Tim
turns.text: It’s the right one. By supper I want to cut the shoe off.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He had already sought advice and been told to return if the trouble persisted. Different shoes had helped for a little while, then disappointed him.

Roger crouched beside the curb.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: May I look?

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Tim handed him the shoe.

Roger checked the seams, pressed the lining, and ran his thumb around the inside.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I don’t know whether I can solve it,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: he said.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: But there are a few things I could try.

turns.speaker: Tim
turns.text: How much?

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: For looking? Nothing.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Tim studied him.

turns.speaker: Tim
turns.text: Bring it back before Thursday. I need it.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger returned it the following evening.

He had fitted a soft insert beneath the foot.

Two days later, Tim shook his head.

turns.speaker: Tim
turns.text: Comfortable standing still. Worse when I’m driving.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger tried a firmer material.

Then a thinner one.

Then he made removable inserts so Tim could compare them during different parts of the day.

Nothing lasted.

Each time Tim returned disappointed, Roger felt a heaviness in his stomach. At first he worried that Tim would think him useless. Then he watched the man ease his foot out of the shoe, and the embarrassment gave way to something more painful: he wanted to help, and he did not know how.

That night he sat with an unfinished insert before him.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: God, I have reached the end of what I know. You haven’t. Help me understand what this man needs.
turns.instruction: A personal prayer addressed to God. Speak as a real man in this moment, with vulnerability, longing, gratitude or growing trust as the words imply. Expressive and understated, never preaching. No whispering.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He rested his tired hands on the bench. He stopped trying to invent a brilliant answer for a moment and read Tim’s words again.

Roger began keeping notes on scraps of paper: where the pain appeared, how long Tim had driven, which shoe he wore.

At night, he laid the scraps beside his tools.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Please help me understand what I’m missing.
turns.instruction: A sincere private prayer. Let the specific meaning guide the emotion: fear, longing, gratitude or trust. Clearly voiced, not whispered or sermon-like.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Once, after another unsuccessful fitting, he offered to stop.

Tim leaned against the car.

turns.speaker: Tim
turns.text: You remember what I tell you,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: he said.

turns.speaker: Tim
turns.text: Most people just tell me to buy another pair.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
So Roger continued.

He tried shoes with almost no cushioning. He changed the flexibility of the soles. He adjusted the room around the toes.

Then, one morning, he made a mistake.

Two nearly identical trial pairs stood beneath his bench. In his hurry, he packed a left shoe from one pair and a right shoe from the other.

Tim wore them for an entire working day.

That evening, he arrived at Roger’s door still wearing both shoes.

turns.speaker: Tim
turns.text: What did you change?

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Roger felt his stomach tighten.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Why?

turns.speaker: Tim
turns.text: Because I’ve just driven six hours, and I’m not desperate to take this one off.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger examined the pair.

The left shoe had the cushioned insert.

The right had the thinner, firmer footbed.

He did not understand everything about it. But he remembered what Tim had said weeks earlier: the soft cushioning felt worse at the pedals.

He made a second pair with the same arrangement and asked Tim to try it carefully over several days.

The improvement held.

Roger waited until Tim had left before sitting down. Relief came over him so suddenly that his eyes filled.

He had been so certain that he was running out of answers. Yet a possibility had existed that he had never thought to test.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Thank You. I couldn’t see it, but my not seeing it didn’t mean there was nothing there.
turns.instruction: A personal prayer addressed to God. Speak as a real man in this moment, with vulnerability, longing, gratitude or growing trust as the words imply. Expressive and understated, never preaching. No whispering.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He gave thanks for Tim’s patience too. Without that patience, there would have been no next attempt.

Tim began calling them his miracle shoes.

Roger smiled when he heard it, but in his notebook he wrote something more useful:

The two feet did not need the same thing.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Tim told his employer, Rick, while opening the car door.

Rick had watched him limp at the end of enough evenings to notice the difference.

turns.speaker: Rick
turns.text: He really helped you?

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Tim nodded.

turns.speaker: Rick
turns.text: Then I’d like to meet him.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Rick walked every morning. One foot was slightly longer than the other, and buying ordinary pairs meant accepting either cramped toes on one side or a loose heel on the other.

At their first meeting, Roger measured both feet separately.

Rick watched him.

turns.speaker: Rick
turns.text: You seem nervous.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I am.

turns.speaker: Rick
turns.text: About the shoes?

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: About promising more than I can do.

turns.speaker: Rick
turns.text: Then promise what you can.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Roger considered that.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I can promise to keep working until we know whether I can make you something better.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Rick agreed to pay a materials deposit.

Roger had rehearsed asking for it all the way to the house. Rick’s easy acceptance surprised him so much that he briefly forgot the amount.

On the way out, Roger paused with the deposit in his pocket. He had spent the journey imagining humiliation. Instead, he had met willingness.

He thanked God quietly, then wrote down exactly what the money was for. Receiving help made him want to be more careful with what had been entrusted to him.

He spent the next several days visiting shops, examining walking shoes, speaking with suppliers, and studying how different soles bent beneath the ball of the foot.

He could not afford to buy everything he wanted to study. Some shopkeepers let him look. One dismissed him. A repairer across town showed him several worn pairs and explained where they had failed.

When Roger returned to Rick, he brought trial uppers and several combinations of footbeds and soles.

They tested five arrangements that afternoon.

Two felt promising.

Over the following fortnight, Roger made a finished pair and adjusted it after Rick’s walks.

When Rick finally said,

turns.speaker: Rick
turns.text: Leave them exactly as they are,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger felt a satisfaction that stayed with him the whole journey home.

Rick paid the balance, then added a substantial bonus. The total was roughly ten times the original materials deposit.

Roger stared at the money.

Rick mistook his silence.

turns.speaker: Rick
turns.text: Is something wrong?

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Rick
turns.text: Good. My wife would like to see you.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Katie received him in a room with more shoes than Roger had ever seen outside a shop.

Beside her stood a young woman carrying a notebook.

turns.speaker: Katie
turns.text: This is Rita,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Katie said.

turns.speaker: Katie
turns.text: She keeps me from arriving at appointments on the wrong day.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Rita smiled.

Roger nearly dropped his measuring tape.

Katie wanted evening slippers: elegant, fitted properly, and decorated with ornaments she already owned.

She opened a small box.

Inside lay a pair of jeweled pieces shaped like leaves.

Roger had never held anything so valuable.

Katie described how she wanted them to catch the light when she walked.

He listened, then set the box down carefully.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I need to tell you something. I haven’t made anything like this before.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Katie waited.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I understand leather and fitting. I’ll need help with the ornament work.

turns.speaker: Katie
turns.text: Can you find it?

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I believe I can.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Rita looked up from her notebook.

It was the first time Roger had heard himself say those words without immediately explaining why he might be wrong.

Katie took him shopping to show him the shapes she liked. Roger paid attention to things he had once barely noticed: the curve of an opening, how a narrow strap changed the look of a foot, the difference between decoration that seemed graceful and decoration that seemed heavy.

He used part of Rick’s payment to buy materials and pay for instruction.

Then the trouble began.

The first sample looked clumsy.

On the second, the decorated leather pulled out of shape.

He tested a mounting method with inexpensive imitation pieces. It held when the slipper sat on his bench and loosened when someone walked in it.

The money disappeared faster than he expected.

Some nights he looked at the ruined pieces and felt foolish for ever having believed he could do this. The ornaments seemed to belong to a world into which he had wandered by mistake.

He bowed his head over the bench.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: God, I’m frightened. I want to hide from her. Please help me be honest, and help me find the knowledge I don’t have.
turns.instruction: A personal prayer addressed to God. Speak as a real man in this moment, with vulnerability, longing, gratitude or growing trust as the words imply. Expressive and understated, never preaching. No whispering.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He had asked for a solution. What he found himself able to do first was send an honest message.

He still took factory shifts. His mother sometimes found him asleep beside the lamp, a scrap of leather in one hand.

For three days, ashamed of his lack of progress, he avoided sending Katie an update.

On the fourth, he wrote to her.

The attachment is not strong enough yet. I won’t put your ornaments at risk. I need more time.

Her reply was brief.

Thank you for telling me. Show me when it is ready.

He folded that note and kept it.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
The solution began in a jeweler’s cramped workshop.

Roger had already visited two people who said the job was not worth their time.

The third listened.

Roger felt the impulse to explain how much he already knew. He let it go.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Help me listen,
turns.instruction: A personal prayer addressed to God. Speak as a real man in this moment, with vulnerability, longing, gratitude or growing trust as the words imply. Expressive and understated, never preaching. No whispering.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
he asked inwardly.

The jeweler drew something on a scrap of paper. Roger leaned closer. Here was a mind trained by years he had never lived, seeing a possibility he had missed. He felt gratitude before he knew whether the suggestion would work.

Instead of fastening the ornaments directly through the thin slipper upper, the jeweler suggested mounting them in small settings attached to a separate, reinforced leather panel.

Together, they positioned the decoration on a part of the upper that flexed less. The jeweler smoothed the metal fittings. Roger enclosed the backs beneath a soft lining so that nothing sharp touched the foot.

He practiced with imitation ornaments first.

He bent the samples, pulled at them, and asked his sister to walk around the house in a trial pair while he watched for movement.

Only then did they fit Katie’s pieces.

When Roger brought the slippers to her, she lifted one toward the window.

turns.speaker: Katie
turns.text: Oh, Roger.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
For a moment, he thought he had finished.

Then she walked across the room.

Her smile changed.

turns.speaker: Katie
turns.text: They press here.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
She touched the front of her foot.

Roger felt the familiar disappointment rise in him.

Rita was watching from beside the doorway.

He could have explained how many weeks the decoration had taken. He could have suggested that evening shoes were never entirely comfortable.

Instead, he knelt.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Show me exactly where.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
His disappointment had not disappeared. He could feel it while he waited for her answer.

But he remembered God there too, kneeling beside a customer’s chair, with the work he had hoped was finished beginning again. He asked for the patience to care more about her comfort than about being praised.

He marked the spot.

The next version had more room through the forefoot, a smoother lining, and thin cushioning placed where Katie needed it rather than spread everywhere.

She walked across the room.

Then back again.

Then she kept walking.

This time, Roger waited for her to speak.

turns.speaker: Katie
turns.text: When can you make another pair?

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Katie wanted heels next.

Roger sought out a maker who understood balance and heel construction. He paid for the man’s time and accepted being a beginner again.

There were failed samples. There were fittings that looked right and felt wrong. There was a heel position he changed by a small amount that made a surprisingly large difference.

Throughout it, he prayed.

Sometimes the prayer was hopeful.

Sometimes it was simply,

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Help me stay patient.
turns.instruction: A sincere private prayer. Let the specific meaning guide the emotion: fear, longing, gratitude or trust. Clearly voiced, not whispered or sermon-like.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
When Katie settled his fees for the slippers, the heels, and the development work, she added a bonus that left him speechless.

It was about ten times what Rick had paid him.

More than Roger had earned in the factory in a year.

He counted it at home with his mother beside him.

Then he counted it again.

His mother did not ask what he would buy.

She said,

turns.speaker: Mother
turns.text: Put aside what belongs to the work.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
They separated the money: household needs, materials, wages owed to the craftsmen who had helped him, savings.

For the first time, there was still a meaningful amount left.

He looked at the remaining money, then at the piles that would pay other people. The payment had fed more than one household. The jeweler had earned something. The other maker had earned something. Katie had received shoes she loved.

Roger had once imagined prosperity as a small locked room in which a few people kept what everyone else needed. This felt different. Something useful had come into existence, and several lives were better because of it.

For him, this was a glimpse of the abundance he had prayed to recognize. God had not become more generous that month. Roger had begun to see more ways to receive, work with, and pass on that generosity.

Roger sat quietly before it.

He had not taken it from anyone.

He had listened, learned, asked for help, and made something another person valued.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Thank you, God,
turns.instruction: A sincere private prayer. Let the specific meaning guide the emotion: fear, longing, gratitude or trust. Clearly voiced, not whispered or sermon-like.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: he said.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Katie’s friends began asking about the shoes.

At first, Roger took one commission at a time.

Then there were more appointments than he could manage after his shifts.

Katie approached her father, who owned several businesses.

She brought him orders, cost estimates, and samples. He asked difficult questions. Some she could answer. Others she brought back to Roger.

Eventually, they agreed to fund a small company.

Katie would run the commercial side and bring in customers. Her father would provide capital and advice. Roger would lead design, fitting, and production.

Roger’s share would be thirty percent.

Before signing, he paid an independent adviser to explain the agreement.

It cost him money he disliked spending.

He was glad afterward that he had spent it.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
The workshop frightened him more than his first private commission.

Now mistakes could waste other people’s wages.

He knew how to work at a production bench. He had never designed the flow of an entire workshop.

He stood in the empty room the evening before the equipment arrived.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Help me build something good here,
turns.instruction: A sincere private prayer. Let the specific meaning guide the emotion: fear, longing, gratitude or trust. Clearly voiced, not whispered or sermon-like.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: he prayed.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Help me recognize what I don’t know.
turns.instruction: A sincere private prayer. Let the specific meaning guide the emotion: fear, longing, gratitude or trust. Clearly voiced, not whispered or sermon-like.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He hired a cutter whose precision he had admired for years, an experienced stitcher, and a production supervisor who had organized work in another factory.

Together, they divided the process into stages: measuring and fitting, patterns, cutting, stitching, assembly, finishing, inspection.

They labeled each customer’s measurements clearly. They kept separate patterns for left and right feet when required. They checked a trial fitting before completing expensive custom work.

Roger made mistakes.

Once, he moved a workstation because it looked tidier and slowed the whole room down.

The supervisor explained why.

Roger moved it back.

The employees began offering suggestions more freely after that.

Remembrance began to find a place in the smallest parts of his day. Before cutting costly leather, he asked for care in his hands. When a needle snapped and irritation rose, he paused before speaking to the person beside him. When someone caught an error, he thanked God for the correction and thanked the person aloud.

Sometimes he forgot for hours. He became hurried, proud of a design, frightened by a bill. Then he would notice the tightness in himself and return, without ceremony.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Help me with this too.
turns.instruction: A personal prayer addressed to God. Speak as a real man in this moment, with vulnerability, longing, gratitude or growing trust as the words imply. Expressive and understated, never preaching. No whispering.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: A tangled thread. A difficult apology. A decision about wages. He was learning that he did not have to wait for a crisis to turn toward God.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Their first serious business failure arrived in beautiful boxes.

Dozens of them.

Stacked against a wall.

Katie’s friends had loved the early designs, and Roger had assumed that more shoes would mean more sales.

They had committed too much money to too many styles.

Some sizes hardly moved. Certain colors received compliments and no orders. Materials sat unused while wages and rent continued to fall due.

Roger began arriving before everyone else and leaving after they had gone.

One evening, his mother found him at the kitchen table studying figures.

turns.speaker: Mother
turns.text: Are we in trouble?

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He almost said no.

Instead, he told her what was happening.

After she went to bed, he remained at the table. He had prayed before opening the workshop. He had worked until his eyes hurt. Why was he sitting here afraid of losing it?

For a moment, he felt ashamed even of the question. Then he brought that to God as well.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I thought I was doing the right thing. I don’t understand this. Please help me. Help me see clearly enough to protect the people depending on me.
turns.instruction: A personal prayer addressed to God. Speak as a real man in this moment, with vulnerability, longing, gratitude or growing trust as the words imply. Expressive and understated, never preaching. No whispering.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He wanted certainty that everything would be all right. None came.

What returned, slowly, was the recognition that his fear did not know everything. These figures described a problem. They did not describe the limits of God. There might be a question he had not asked, an error he had not understood, a person from whom he could learn.

He could not see the whole way forward. He could ask for help with tomorrow.

The next morning, he went to Katie’s father.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I know how to make something one person wants,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Roger said.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I don’t know how to make enough people buy it.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: The older man closed the notebook between them.

turns.speaker: Katie’s father
turns.text: Then you have another trade to learn.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He advised them to reduce the range, protect their cash, and stop making speculative stock until they understood demand.

Then he asked Roger a question.

turns.speaker: Katie’s father
turns.text: When did you last speak to someone who bought from you?

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Roger named a customer he had fitted that week.

turns.speaker: Katie’s father
turns.text: After the sale, I mean.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger had no answer.

Heat rose into his face. Then, beneath the embarrassment, he felt a small opening. There was something he could do that he had not been doing.

He silently thanked God for bringing him to a question that humbled him enough to learn.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He began making visits.

He asked before calling. He wrote down preferences. He checked whether shoes had remained comfortable after an entire evening, not merely during a fitting.

He learned that one customer loved her slippers but never wore them because the color matched nothing she owned.

Another needed shoes for a particular gala and had ordered elsewhere because she had not known Roger could deliver in time.

One woman said quietly that she hated having to choose between looking elegant and being able to remain on her feet beside her friends.

Roger remembered that.

He and Katie arranged small appointments where customers could see samples, bring their dresses, and discuss upcoming events.

They improved the packaging so the shoes arrived protected, beautifully presented, and accompanied by clear care instructions.

They asked satisfied customers for introductions. They made alterations promptly. They developed a small collection that customers could adapt instead of beginning every design from nothing.

For the next season, they took deposits before committing to larger material orders.

The unsold boxes gradually disappeared.

More importantly, fewer new ones accumulated.

Roger discovered that selling could be another form of attention.

He did not have to become someone else.

He had to keep listening after the shoes left his hands.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Before a visit, he would ask God to help him hear what mattered to the customer. Afterward, he gave thanks for what she had told him, even when it was criticism.

The world was beginning to feel larger. There were more needs than he could serve alone, more designs than he could make in a lifetime, more people with knowledge to share. He did not need to possess all of it. He could take his place in it, do useful work, and trust that the source of abundance was greater than his grasp.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Rita appeared often during those months.

Sometimes she accompanied Katie. Sometimes she collected an order for another woman she assisted.

Roger learned that her family had once been wealthy. A business failure had changed their circumstances, and she had gone to work.

She spoke of it without bitterness.

One afternoon, while waiting for a small alteration, she helped his mother carry a basket through the workshop door.

Later, his mother said,

turns.speaker: Mother
turns.text: That young woman has good manners.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger pretended to be occupied.

His mother noticed.

Rita once found him apologizing for the plain room where he received fittings.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: It isn’t much yet,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
he said.

She looked around at the measured patterns, the clean workbench, and the half-finished shoes.

turns.speaker: Rita
turns.text: People are doing honest work here.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: He glanced at her.

turns.speaker: Rita
turns.text: There’s nothing to apologize for,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
she said.

He remembered that sentence long after he forgot what they had discussed afterward.

That evening, he remembered her kindness while putting away his tools. He thanked God for it as simply as he might have thanked Him for food.

He was beginning to recognize provision in things he could not deposit in an account: a word that relieved his shame, a person who understood his mother, the courage to be seen before his work was perfect.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
The company’s growth took years.

There were seasons when orders came easily and seasons when Roger worried again.

A supplier failed to deliver. A promising design sold poorly. A large order had to be remade because a material behaved differently in use than it had in the sample.

But the business learned.

Roger learned.

His reputation spread beyond the city. Customers traveled for fittings. Invitations arrived from retailers and event organizers. People began asking what he would make next.

They paid high prices because the work was distinctive, the fit received unusual care, and Roger’s company had earned a reputation for putting problems right.

He paid his employees reliably. He promoted people who could do things better than he could. He gave the workshop time for training and allowed experienced hands to question a design before it became an expensive mistake.

His days remained disciplined.

He began them in prayer.

He still carried a notebook.

And when a customer described a problem, he tried to hear it before deciding he already knew the answer.

Success did not remove his need for that inward return. Sometimes it made the need harder to notice. An important customer praised him, and he would carry the words around all afternoon. A worker questioned him, and he would feel himself stiffen.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
When he caught it, he asked God to keep him teachable. He remembered the first insert that had failed, the jeweler’s drawing, the supervisor who had moved the workstation back.

His skill was real. So was the help through which it had grown. Remembering both allowed him to enjoy what he could do without imagining that everything depended on him.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Success brought attention he had never expected.

Some invitations were innocent. Others were not.

Once, a married customer suggested that he bring samples to her house late in the evening, when her husband would be away.

Roger recognized the invitation beneath the words.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: We can arrange a fitting at the showroom,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: he said gently.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Katie will help us choose a convenient time.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
When she pressed, he remained courteous and firm.

Afterward, he told no entertaining story about it.

Her private embarrassment was not something he wanted to turn into his own importance.

He found that wealth gave him more choices.

He wanted to remain responsible for the choices he made.

Before answering invitations that stirred his vanity, he sometimes needed a moment alone.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: God, help me choose what will leave peace in my home and in theirs.
turns.instruction: A personal prayer addressed to God. Speak as a real man in this moment, with vulnerability, longing, gratitude or growing trust as the words imply. Expressive and understated, never preaching. No whispering.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Then he returned and spoke kindly. The remembrance belonged there as much as it belonged beside his prayer mat.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
In time, Roger saved enough to purchase a larger share of the company.

He did not empty the business to do it.

With retained personal earnings and a formally arranged loan from clients who had come to trust him, he negotiated to buy another thirty percent. Advisers reviewed the terms. The repayments were measured against what he could reasonably afford.

The papers were signed in the same office where he had once struggled to explain his first cost estimates.

Afterward, Katie shook his hand.

Then she laughed.

turns.speaker: Katie
turns.text: You still look as though you’ve been called into trouble.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger laughed too.

Some habits took longer to change than others.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He bought a spacious house with a garden his mother could tend if she wished, and rooms where his siblings could return with families of their own.

There were vehicles now. There were journeys he could once only have imagined.

He enjoyed them.

He enjoyed buying good materials without first calculating whether it would leave the household short. He enjoyed paying for his brother’s studies. He enjoyed giving his mother the freedom to choose something because she liked it.

Abundance had become more than a sum in an account.

It was room to act.

Room to rest.

Room to help without panic.

He no longer apologized inwardly for enjoying it. When his mother chose something beautiful for the house, he delighted in her pleasure. When his brother wrote about his studies, Roger read the letter twice.

He wanted a full life: worthwhile work, a generous home, comfort, beauty, love, and the means to do more good. He could bring those desires to God openly.

He knew the company had limits. His time and judgment had limits. God did not. He could respect the limits of a particular plan without surrendering his belief in the vastness of what remained possible.

That recognition made him grateful for what he held and hopeful about what he had yet to discover.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: When his mother finally mentioned marriage, she did so while pouring tea.

turns.speaker: Mother
turns.text: There is someone I would like you to consider.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Roger kept his eyes on his cup.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Who?

turns.speaker: Mother
turns.text: Rita.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: He looked up so quickly that she smiled.

turns.speaker: Mother
turns.text: I would speak to her family,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: she said.

turns.speaker: Mother
turns.text: If you wished. And if she wished.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He asked for a day to think.

His mother gave him until the following morning.

When Roger and Rita met to speak seriously, he was more nervous than he had been in several important business meetings.

She made it easier by admitting that she was nervous too.

Roger felt his shoulders loosen. He silently thanked God for that small kindness. He had prayed over large sums of money with more composure than he had managed while waiting for her to arrive.

They spoke about faith, family, work, and the kind of home they wanted.

Roger told her that he did not want her to feel she had to hide the years when her family had struggled.

turns.speaker: Rita
turns.text: I don’t,

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: she said.

turns.speaker: Rita
turns.text: We worked. We were honest. God was there too.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He knew then that his mother had understood something he had been too shy to say aloud.

They married with the willing blessing of both families.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Years later, Roger came home after a long day and found the house quiet.

Rita had left a lamp burning.

His mother had fallen asleep in her chair with a book resting open in her lap.

For a moment, he stood in the doorway.

He remembered her hands dividing his wages into small piles.

He remembered the landlord’s notice beneath the salt jar.

He remembered a man in a factory asking who would feed her when he failed.

Roger lifted the book and marked her place.

She stirred.

turns.speaker: Mother
turns.text: You’re home?

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Yes, Mother.

turns.speaker: Mother
turns.text: Have you eaten?

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: He smiled.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
She settled back.

There was nothing she needed to calculate that night.

Roger stood beside her until her breathing grew steady again.

Gratitude rose through him with the memory of all those small, frightened prayers: beside the factory bench, outside a stranger’s door, over a shoe that would not come right.

He had not known, while living them, how one day would lead to another. He had only known where to turn.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: Thank You for caring for us in ways I could not imagine.
turns.instruction: A personal prayer addressed to God. Speak as a real man in this moment, with vulnerability, longing, gratitude or growing trust as the words imply. Expressive and understated, never preaching. No whispering.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He drew the blanket gently over her knees. Then he switched off the brighter lamp and left the softer one burning.

The next morning, he rose before the household.

There was a difficult fitting waiting at the workshop. A new employee needed guidance. A customer had written about a fastening that troubled her fingers.

He washed, knelt, and prayed.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text:
Thank you for what You have given us.

Help me care for it well.

And show me where I can be useful today.
turns.instruction: A sincere private prayer. Let the specific meaning guide the emotion: fear, longing, gratitude or trust. Clearly voiced, not whispered or sermon-like.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Then he stood up and went to work.
